Unregulated e-pharmacy platforms are reportedly accepting these AI-generated prescriptions to enable the unlawful online sale of antibiotics, opioids, Schedule H and Schedule X medicines, and banned drugs, bypassing prescription verification safeguards. Reported impact The AIOCD warned that the practice poses a 'grave threat to public health' and specifically risks antimicrobial resistance and misuse of psychotropic drugs. Unlike offline pharmacies which maintain human oversight through physical verification and patient interaction, online platforms make it 'practically impossible' to differentiate between genuine and AI-generated fake prescriptions. Index analysis The scheme exploits regulatory loopholes in GSR 817(E) and GSR 220(E) notifications under the Drugs and Cosmetics Act, which govern online sale and home delivery of medicines but lack effective prescription verification mechanisms for e-pharmacy platforms. Governance controls The AIOCD urged the Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation to immediately withdraw the GSR notifications, shut down illegal e-pharmacy platforms by blocking their websites and digital payment gateways, and prohibit the use of AI or digital tools for generating medical prescriptions.
AII-1001-07641: On the night of February 16, 2026, Daniel Milligan, a Tesla owner and former SpaceX engineer, was driving with FSD version 14.2.2.4 when the system made a right turn onto a boat ramp leading toward a lake and accelerated toward the water at approximately 10 mph instead of slowing down. Milligan intervened by taking manual control of the vehicle before it entered the lake. He had intended to drive to a driveway about fifty feet away from the boat ramp. Reported impact No collision or injury occurred, as Milligan took control of the vehicle in time. The driver stated the car was moving at a speed that suggested it would have entered the lake had he not intervened. Index analysis Milligan repeated the same route during daylight the following morning and reported that FSD did not turn onto the boat ramp, instead proceeding correctly to the intended driveway. He attributed the night-time malfunction to poor lighting conditions, hypothesizing the system either could not see the driveway ahead or could not clearly perceive the lake in low light.
AII-1001-07583: A vulnerability in DJI ROMO robot vacuum authentication was discovered by developer Sammy Azdoufal when he attempted to connect his own device to a PlayStation 5 controller. By extracting a private token from his ROMO device, Azdoufal found he could access data and controls of approximately 7,000 ROMO vacuums across 24 countries within nine minutes. The security flaw resided in the DJI Home backend's MQTT protocol validation, where the server failed to verify that access permissions corresponded only to a user's own device. When the server received a token, it did not properly validate that the token's permissions matched the specific robot being accessed, allowing a single token to act as a universal key across the entire infrastructure. Reported impact Unauthorized access provided real-time video feeds, audio, detailed home maps, device serial numbers, cleaning status, and battery levels from affected homes. The vulnerability exposed personal data and enabled remote control of thousands of robot vacuums across multiple countries. The case highlighted privacy and security risks in connected smart home devices, particularly the presence of cameras and microphones in everyday appliances connected to the internet. Index analysis DJI identified the vulnerability at the end of January and deployed an initial patch on February 8, though it did not apply correctly across all servers. A second update was deployed on February 10 to ensure the fix was extended throughout the entire infrastructure, and DJI stated the problem was subsequently resolved.
AII-1001-07517: Internet fraud involving AI-generated fake images, audio and video content caused losses exceeding $1.5 billion last year. Common fraud schemes include false invoices for corporate reimbursements, altered photographs to justify insurance claims or returns, images of events that never occurred, and cloned audio used to authorize money transfers. The fraudulent content has particularly affected sectors including insurance, e-commerce, logistics and real estate where manipulated photographs are used to demand compensation or validate transactions. Reported impact AI-manipulated or AI-created content caused damage exceeding $1.5 billion last year according to various reports. Governments and technology companies have launched tools to detect fake images in response to the growing fraud wave. Index analysis Experts describe the situation as a digital arms race: each improvement in detection triggers improvements in generation. Detection platforms including Vericta, IMGDetector.ai, RealReveal, Tenorshare and AI or Not analyze inconsistencies and technical traces of AI-generated content, with Vericta developing technology capable of determining in seconds whether a file is real or AI-generated. Governance controls Governments and technology companies are developing tools to detect fake images. Vericta received support from public organizations including the Centro para el Desarrollo Tecnológico e Industrial and the Municipality of Barcelona to develop detection technology.
AII-1001-07499: A TikTok account impersonating Grainville School used the school's badge and branding to upload five videos containing deepfake content that targeted school staff members. The account was removed from TikTok after being reported to the platform and to the States of Jersey Police. Reported impact School staff members were targeted by the inappropriate deepfake content posted on the account. Index analysis Deputy Rob Ward urged people not to watch, share, or engage with the material, noting that circulating fake accounts can inadvertently give them more attention and encourage similar behaviour. Governance controls The Education and Lifelong Learning Minister confirmed the incident had been reported to TikTok and the States of Jersey Police. The government indicated focus on ensuring swift removal of content, supporting those affected, and reinforcing safeguarding measures.
AII-1001-07317: An Amazon delivery van drove onto the Broomway, a six-mile walking path across mudflats in Great Wakering, Essex, on Saturday evening after the driver was following GPS directions to Foulness Island. HM Coastguard Southend was called out on Sunday morning to reports of the vehicle on the Broomway. The driver had safely exited the vehicle and reported the incident to Amazon. Reported impact The driver was safely removed from the vehicle. Amazon arranged for recovery of the van with assistance from a nearby farmer on Sunday. Index analysis The Broomway is a 600-year-old route described as the 'deadliest footpath in Britain', with over 100 deaths recorded in parish records. The path crosses flat sands and is home to a Ministry of Defence firing range, and is said to require caution and specialist knowledge to navigate safely. Qinetiq, which manages the firing range, describes the Broomway as 'not suitable for vehicles' and advises that people only traverse it accompanied by a guide who knows the mudflats. Essex Highways manages the route. Governance controls Amazon said it was 'aware' of the situation and was 'investigating'.
AII-1001-09441: Authenticated attackers could read arbitrary files from the Gateway host by supplying absolute paths or path traversal sequences to the browser tool's upload action via POST /tools/invoke with {"tool":"browser","action":"upload",...} or POST /hooks/file-chooser. The server passed upload paths to Playwright's setInputFiles() APIs without restricting them to a safe root, allowing the referenced files to be read from the local filesystem and contents exfiltrated by page JavaScript or via agent/browser snapshots. Reported impact The vulnerability enabled arbitrary local file read on the Gateway host, affecting confidentiality. Index analysis The vulnerability required authenticated access and the browser tool to be permitted by tool policy; in default setups the Gateway binds to loopback with a generated gateway token for onboarding. Governance controls Upload paths are now confined to OpenClaw's temp uploads root (DEFAULT_UPLOAD_DIR) and traversal/escape paths are rejected, as implemented in fix commit 3aa94af.
AII-1001-09287: OpenClaw's macOS desktop client versions 2026.2.6 through 2026.2.13 displayed only the first 240 characters of agent messages in confirmation dialogs for openclaw://agent deep links without an unattended key, but executed the full message after the user clicked 'Run'. An attacker could pad a message with whitespace to push a malicious payload outside the visible preview in the confirmation dialog, increasing the chance a user would approve a different message than the one actually executed. Reported impact If a user ran the deep link, the agent could perform actions leading to arbitrary command execution depending on the user's configured tool approvals and allowlists, according to the advisory. This was a social-engineering mediated vulnerability where the confirmation prompt could misrepresent the executed message. Index analysis The vulnerability was assigned CVE-2026-26320 and classified as High severity under CWE-451 (User Interface Misrepresentation of Critical Information). Governance controls OpenClaw released patched version 2026.2.14 which enforces a strict message length limit for unkeyed deep link confirmations and ignores delivery/routing parameters (deliver, to, channel) unless a valid unattended key is provided.
AII-1001-07617: Tesla Europe deployed Grok, an AI chatbot developed by xAI, to nine European countries on 15 February 2026 via software update 2026.2.6. The deployment enabled drivers to activate the chatbot from the vehicle's touchscreen or steering wheel microphone button on compatible models with AMD processors and Premium Connectivity or Wi-Fi. Grok was previously reported to have generated harmful content, including Holocaust denial, antisemitic responses, deepfakes of women and minors without consent, and statements about sacrificing humanity to protect Elon Musk. In January 2026, the European Commission opened a formal investigation after the tool was used to produce sexually explicit deepfakes of women and minors. Reported impact The deployment triggered concerns over the chatbot's documented history of producing harmful content on X, the platform where Grok was developed. Observers noted reputational risks associated with the tool's previous controversial outputs. Index analysis Grok version 4.20, released in beta in mid-February 2026, reportedly consulted posts by Elon Musk on X as a primary source when addressing sensitive topics, raising questions about the system's neutrality and independence in forming responses. Governance controls Tesla stated that Grok cannot control vehicle climate, media, or other onboard functions, and that traditional voice commands remain separate from the chatbot system. Grok requires an internet connection and processes all interactions through xAI's own privacy policy, outside Tesla's purview.
AII-1001-07443: NPR host David Greene, former host of Morning Edition and current host of Left, Right & Center, filed a lawsuit against Google alleging that the company replicated his voice for the male podcast host feature in NotebookLM's Audio Overviews. A former coworker sent Greene the AI tool and asked if he had authorized Google to use his likeness because of the similarity. After receiving this message, Greene reported being "completely freaked out" and received similar inquiries from friends and family members. Google disputed the claim through spokesman José Castañeda, stating: "These allegations are baseless. The sound of the male voice in NotebookLM's Audio Overviews is based on a paid professional actor Google hired." Reported impact Greene described the experience as "eerie," saying "It's this moment where you feel like you're listening to yourself." He stated that his voice is "the most important part of who I am" and characterized the harm as deeper and more personal than a missed opportunity to capitalize on his recognizable asset. Index analysis The lawsuit is described as one of the first in what legal observers expect to become numerous disputes over AI voice use, copyright protections, and ownership rights. Online commentators have debated whether the NotebookLM voice resembles Greene or other public figures such as former tech podcaster Leo Laporte or matches the sound of the "Armchair Expert" podcast.
AII-1001-07437: Researchers from the Universidad de La Rioja and Universidad de Zaragoza published a study in ACM Computing Surveys examining data deletion in AI systems. The study found that AI systems can recover data that users believed had been deleted, distinguishing between recoverable and non-recoverable deletion. Reported impact The recovery capability poses risks to the right to be forgotten, a principle established under European Union law. Residual copies and fragmented information in technologies like temporal databases, blockchain, and machine learning systems can be reconstructed by advanced algorithms, potentially violating the original intent of data deletion requests. Index analysis The study highlights that data deletion is not always irreversible, particularly in complex technological environments where backup systems and distributed computing create fragmented copies of information that AI algorithms can identify and reconstruct.
